name: usage
summary: Plan-allowance meter: records the 5-hour, weekly and spend windows, speaks only near a ceiling, and reports what a cut would save

settings.summary: Where the plan-allowance meter shows: the status line, the session-start line, both, or nowhere.
settings.detail:
off     nothing is displayed. Readings are still recorded, so turning it
        back on later has a history behind it
status  the line under the prompt only, and only near a ceiling
login   one line at session start only
both    both of the above  (default)

The meter is deliberately silent in ordinary use. A line that is always
there is read for a day and then never again -- the failure gt_closeout
already demonstrated by asking the same question every session until the
answer stopped being read. It speaks when a number has crossed a point
where a person would do something about it.

The status line needs one entry in settings.json that no installer can
write for you, because it is the user's own display:

  "statusLine": {"type": "command",
                 "command": "python3 ~/.claude/golden-thread/hooks/gt_usage.py"}

settings.summary: How close to a ceiling the allowance must be before the meter says anything — or `always`, to keep it on screen permanently.
settings.detail:
early   5-hour 50%, weekly 40%, spend 50%, context 70%
normal  5-hour 80%, weekly 75%, spend 75%, context 85%  (default)
late    5-hour 90%, weekly 90%, spend 90%, context 95%
always  show every render, whatever the numbers

`always` is for someone who wants the meter in view while they work, and it
is deliberately not the default. A line that is always there is read for a
day and then never again -- the failure gt_closeout demonstrated by asking
the same question every session until the answer stopped being read. Chosen
deliberately it is useful; arrived at by default it becomes furniture.

A window a plan does not report is never shown, and never shown as 0%:
absent and zero are different facts. On a plan with no monthly spend cap the
spend threshold is wired and inert, which the readout says plainly rather
than implying a third alarm is standing guard.

What the meter is NOT is a cost saver. Cache writes count toward API rate
limits and cache reads do not; whether either touches a subscription
allowance is undocumented. Measured on one machine over 180 days, 65% of
cache-write volume was avoidable -- and the weekly window still sat at 13%,
so the waste was real and the scarcity was not.
